result.explanation: A $500 Amazon eGift Card was bought on 2025-02-21. Policy §V.B.1.d prohibits gift certificates except for employee recognition. In the card history I reviewed (Nov 2024–Mar 2025), the card buys office supplies, shipping, telecom and software. It shows no other gift cards and no recognition program. The eGift Card is the only one in that window, and the exception isn't supported by this card's data.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.d — Gift Certificates (except purchases for employee recognition)
result.innocent_explanation: The gift card may have been an employee recognition award, which the policy allows. An approval or recognition program record, or the purchase request, would show that. I did not see that in this card's history.

result.explanation: Single $4,850 charge for SketchUp Pro and V-Ray licenses, under the $5,000 limit. No other Creation Engine charges on this card within the window, so no split or double charge. Software matches the card's main categories (36 software purchases). The July 17 McNeel charge is a different vendor and product. Creation Engine is a software reseller used by this agency.
result.policy_clause: OMES P-Card Procedures §IV.D — $5,000 single item purchase limit
result.innocent_explanation: Bulk academic licensing of design software (SketchUp Pro School, V-Ray) bought as one order under the single-purchase limit.

result.explanation: Quartzy is a lab-supply marketplace and this card's top merchant (615 charges, median card purchase $250, many daily). The numeric suffixes (e.g. 6020199733904, 6020200978456) recur across different days and amounts, so they look like account or sub-account codes, not single order references. Descriptions differ (MEM, tubes, Cremophor). No evidence of one known quantity split to evade $5,000.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing (known quantity and intent are key)
result.innocent_explanation: Routine high-volume lab supply buying through Quartzy, which bundles many vendors' items. Separate requisitions from different lab members or projects over several days are consistent with this card's steady daily pattern.

result.explanation: Hotel room charges at a Long Beach Hyatt fit this card's conference and association spending (AFDO, FOOD ASSN, educational services). The amount is within the merchant's normal range (max $1,719.71). A second charge of $1,719.71 posted the same day, but the amounts differ, so it is not a double charge. Combined $3,282.61 is far below the card's largest purchase, so it is not a limit-evading split.
result.innocent_explanation: Lodging for a group at a conference, booked as separate room folios for different travelers or stays.

result.explanation: A single $3,420 charge for an annual Pope Tech web accessibility subscription, a business software service. The card has two Pope Tech purchases of the same amount, which fits an annual renewal. The card also buys other software and accessibility-related items (Articulate, Elementor, G3ICT). I found no split, no prohibited category and no personal-use pattern.
result.innocent_explanation: Annual renewal of a web accessibility testing subscription, with a 5% discount noted in the description.

result.explanation: Four Amazon charges on 2024-02-19 share one order reference (S821H21P3) and an identical description. Each is under $5,000, but together they total $10,871.04, which is over the limit. This looks like one order billed in parts. The card's later Amazon buying is small (tens to hundreds of dollars), so there is no routine cadence of large charges to explain the cluster.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing: dividing a quantity or failing to consolidate a known quantity to evade the $5,000 limit
result.innocent_explanation: Amazon may have billed a single multi-item order in several shipment-level charges, or the agency may hold an approved exemption for this purchase. An invoice or approval would show this.

result.explanation: Three same-day charges at WINSUPPLY C OKLAHOMA C ($4,341.56, $3,804.57, $4,631.15), each under $5,000, total $12,777.28 — over the limit. Same plumbing category, identical generic descriptions. The card's other charges at this merchant are small (one $881.95), so this is a one-off cluster of large charges, not steady routine buying. Nothing shows the items were unknown at the time of the first purchase.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing
result.innocent_explanation: Three separate jobs or orders for different projects, each unknown when the others were placed. An invoice or order record would show this.

result.explanation: A single $788 charge at a lab-reagent supplier. The card mostly buys lab supplies (DNA oligos, surgical instruments, liquid nitrogen), and this merchant is in the lab/medical category. The agency accounts for most of the merchant's spend (20 purchases). No nearby same-merchant charge, so no split or double charge. $788 is below the card's $2,500 maximum.
result.innocent_explanation: Routine research reagent or assay purchase by a health sciences lab from its usual specialty supplier.

result.explanation: A single $99.82 purchase at Cab Store (outdoor/sporting goods) is below the median for that merchant ($139.48). The Department of Wildlife Conservation is a regular buyer there: 15 purchases across 11 cards, median $116.04. The card mostly buys field and facility supplies (hardware, automotive, tools), so outdoor gear fits. No split, duplicate or prohibited category appears. It is new for this card, but that alone isn't a problem.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.c — Personal Use
result.innocent_explanation: Work gear or supplies for wildlife field staff, bought at a sporting goods store the agency uses regularly.

result.explanation: Three Amazon charges on 2024-09-05 share one order reference (WA5U99MX3) and an identical description (shipping tape, lab notebooks). Each is about $2.4k, under $5,000, but together they total $7,206.38. This card's Amazon buying is normally small (median purchase $224), so these are not routine, steady charges. One reference billed in parts points to a single order split up.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing
result.innocent_explanation: Amazon may have split one large order into several shipments or charges on its own. The cardholder may also have placed separate orders with no known total at the start. The order confirmation and invoice would show this.

result.explanation: The $10.00 charge at "CS QUIKTRIP GC" is coded as POI funding transactions, which is a cash or stored-value load. The "GC" in the name suggests a gift card. Policy §V.B.1.b bars cash and funds transfers, and §V.B.1.d bars gift cards unless they are for employee recognition. This card's history shows no recognition program. It is the card's only QuikTrip charge and the only funding-type charge among 67 transactions, mostly groceries and restaurants.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.b — Cash, including cash advances and ATM transactions (also §V.B.1.d gift cards)
result.innocent_explanation: The $10 could be a gift card bought for an employee recognition award, or a small fuel or snack purchase miscoded as funding. An approval record or the receipt would show which.

result.explanation: A single $600 event registration at Cvent. This fits the card's profile of conferences, memberships and travel (APNA $660, CIHQ summit $372.60, and a $2,800 professional conference). The merchant is used only by this agency, in a small number of purchases, and $600 is the merchant's maximum. I found no repeat charge, split, prohibited category, or personal-looking purchase.
result.innocent_explanation: Conference or event registration fee paid through Cvent for agency staff, consistent with this card's other conference and training purchases.

result.explanation: A single $690.37 stenographic services charge. It is not a split or double charge, because no other INSTASCRIPT charge appears on this card and nothing similar follows within days. The card regularly buys legal items: attorney fees, a Section 1983 handbook, court and county records. The amount is near INSTASCRIPT's median of $537. Stenographic services are not on a prohibited list I saw, and this is a business service, not a consumer purchase.
result.innocent_explanation: Court reporter or transcript service for a legal matter, consistent with this card's other legal purchases and with other state agencies' use of the merchant.

result.explanation: Cell Biolabs is a life-science reagent supplier. This card is a research lab card that regularly buys reagents from VWR, Life Tech, Bio-Rad and Qiagen. The $1,169.93 charge is a single purchase and matches the merchant's typical size (90th percentile $1,169.93; agency median $1,024.93). The card has no other Cell Biolabs charges nearby, so it shows no split or duplicate. It is not prohibited or personal.
result.innocent_explanation: A lab reagent or assay kit order from a specialty life-science vendor, consistent with the card's usual research purchases.

result.explanation: A single $1,420 charge at A.C.E. Testing, a materials testing lab. It is well under the $5,000 limit, with no same-merchant charge nearby, so it is not a split or double charge. $1,420 is the merchant's 90th percentile amount. DOT accounts for 82 of the merchant's 85 purchases, so a testing lab fits an agency that buys this routinely. The card is the only evidence for this DOT card; its largest purchase is $2,012.50.
result.policy_clause: OMES P-Card Procedures §IV.D — $5,000 single purchase limit
result.innocent_explanation: Routine materials or lab testing for DOT, a merchant DOT uses heavily.

result.explanation: Single $4,100 charge at LEGISOK, a legislative publication vendor with 74 purchases across 34 agencies, median $3,350 and max $6,250. The amount is typical for the merchant. The card also buys books, memberships and publications. Another Water Resources Board card bought there, at a median of $4,150. No same-day parts, repeat charge, or prohibited category appears in the history.
result.innocent_explanation: Annual legislative/statute publication subscription typical for state agencies, priced in line with other agencies' purchases.

result.explanation: A single $500 GraphPad Prism academic annual license is ordinary research software for a university card. GraphPad is a common merchant for Oklahoma State University (88 purchases, 5 agencies; median $252, 90th percentile $1,260). The card's only nearby charge is $299 at a different merchant (Grafiti) the day before, so there is no split or duplicate. It's not a prohibited or personal category.
result.innocent_explanation: Annual academic license for GraphPad Prism statistics software, bought for university research or teaching.

result.explanation: A single AT&T telecom bill payment of $728.39. AT&T is a common state vendor: 8,647 purchases, 56 agencies, and 1,302 purchases at this agency. The amount is well under AT&T's 90th percentile of $1,900.65. The card has no other AT&T charges nearby, so there is no split or double charge. Telecom is a business category, not prohibited or personal.
result.innocent_explanation: Routine payment of a departmental AT&T telephone or data service bill.

result.explanation: One $306 purchase at MIAS, a clothing merchant that 302 cards across 16 agencies use, mostly a utility authority, with a median of $190. That pattern fits work or uniform clothing rather than consumer shopping. The card mainly buys facility, plumbing and hardware supplies, and the amount is small and under its $621 median. No split or duplicate appears nearby. Clothing is new for this card, but that alone isn't evidence of personal use.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.c — Personal Use: goods or services for personal use and not for official State use
result.innocent_explanation: Work uniforms, boots or protective clothing bought for facility maintenance staff at a workwear-type vendor.

result.explanation: Four charges at QR-CODE-GENERATOR.COM in three days (Feb 13–15) total $14,554.17, each under $5,000, with the same generic description. This card's only other charges there are two small ones, about $384 combined, so there's no steady cadence of large buys. The merchant's median is $191.88 and its max is $4,822.46, so a cluster of large charges is out of pattern. This looks like one need divided to stay under the limit.
result.policy_clause: OMES Internal P-Card Procedures §V.B.1.a — Split Purchasing: dividing a quantity or failing to consolidate a known quantity to evade the $5,000 limit
result.innocent_explanation: Separate, unrelated software subscriptions or license orders placed on different days, each unknown at the time of the first. An invoice or quote showing distinct orders would clear it.

result.explanation: A single $585.20 fiberglass repair service charge fits this card's marine and boat-related buying (marina, propeller, airboat parts). The agency buys from this merchant regularly (11 purchases, median $711.55). The card has one other charge there, and no same-day or near-day repeat at this merchant. There is no split, double charge, prohibited item or personal-use sign.
result.innocent_explanation: Fiberglass repair work on an agency boat or airboat, consistent with the card's marine purchases and the agency's regular use of this vendor.

result.explanation: Single $3,946.38 charge from Frontiers Media SA, a scholarly open-access publisher. The amount sits at the merchant's 90th percentile (median $2,828.76). OSU has 16 purchases there across 15 cards, so this is routine for the agency. The card has no other Frontiers charge, so no split or double charge. A lab-oriented card buying publication fees fits a business purpose.
result.innocent_explanation: Article publication (open-access) fee paid to a scholarly publisher, typical for university research.

result.explanation: Two identical $54.02 charges at the same Baylor CAVA on consecutive days, both "GENERAL PURCHASE", with no refund or credit. The card has no recurring cadence at this merchant; it appears only on this road trip. A third CAVA charge ($146.73) on 3/30 shows multiple meals, so separate team orders are possible. Nothing in the data confirms that, so this is a likely double charge to recover.
result.policy_clause: Possible double charge: a billing error to recover, not a policy breach
result.innocent_explanation: The team was travelling to Baylor (hotel charges 3/29) and may have bought the same fixed meal order on two days. A receipt would show this.

result.explanation: Two identical $1,499.00 charges at AMAZON RETA K68UU6KE3 on consecutive days, both described "Order Summary item". No refund or credit appears in the card history through 2026-06-12. The card has no recurring $1,499 charge at this merchant. Its other Amazon charges vary in amount and description. This looks like a duplicate billing to recover. A receipt or order confirmation could show two separate orders.
result.policy_clause: Possible double charge: a billing error to recover, not a policy breach
result.innocent_explanation: Two separate Amazon orders for identical $1,499 items (for example, two units of the same equipment) placed on consecutive days. The Amazon order confirmations would show this.

result.explanation: The card is used only for Facebook Ads, with 26 advertising charges. Recurring $900 charges (2024-11-24, 2025-01-25, 02-02, 02-09) fit a steady ad-budget cadence. Each has a different Facebook reference code, and no second $900 charge falls within a few days of the 11-24 one. The agency's other Facebook spending is also routine ad buying. I found no split, double charge, prohibited or personal purchase.
result.innocent_explanation: Routine Facebook ad campaign billing by the health department, charged in the usual $900 ad-spend increments.

result.explanation: A single $1,019.30 charge at AM Leonard, with no other charge at that merchant within 60 days on this card, so no split or double charge. The card mainly buys irrigation, landscape, nursery and construction supplies. AM Leonard is a catalog supplier, and the agency has one other purchase there. The purchase fits the card's grounds-maintenance pattern.
result.innocent_explanation: Routine purchase of grounds or horticulture supplies from a catalog vendor, consistent with the card's usual landscape and irrigation buying.

result.explanation: This card has 207 earlier purchases, mostly industrial supplies, pest control and facility services. It has never bought clothing, and the $1,161.50 charge (T202512011150) has only a generic description. MIAS is used by 16 agencies and 302 cards, mostly a utility with typical amounts around $190 and a $1,475 maximum. That points to workwear or uniforms, but this charge is above typical. An itemized receipt or invoice, with the uniform or approval record, would settle it.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.c — Personal Use: goods or services for personal use and not for official State use
result.innocent_explanation: Work uniforms or protective clothing for staff. MIAS is a clothing merchant that many agencies and cards use, mostly in what looks like a business context.

result.explanation: A $577.06 archery supply purchase on a card that already buys sporting goods (5 transactions, including Lancaster on 2025-06-24 for $227.29 and Shooter's Technology). It fits an OSU 4-H or shooting-sports program. It is a single charge, so there is no split or double charge. The amount is the merchant's median and the agency's typical size. Archery gear is not a prohibited category.
result.innocent_explanation: Routine equipment purchase for a youth shooting-sports or 4-H program from a supplier this card has used before.

result.explanation: The same card was charged $33.54 at WM SUPERCENTER #3615 on 2025-09-30 and again on 2025-10-02. Both have the identical "GENERAL PURCHASE" description. I found no refund or credit in the card history. This card pays Walmart about 13 times in 15 months, so a steady weekly or monthly cadence doesn't explain the pair. This store appears only once more, for $7.06. It is likely a duplicate billing to recover. The amount is small.
result.policy_clause: Possible double charge: a billing error to recover, not a policy breach
result.innocent_explanation: Two separate small grocery runs that happened to total the same amount. A Walmart receipt for each date would show this.

result.explanation: This card is an HVAC/electrical parts card with no clothing purchases in 60 transactions, and nothing in its history explains a $1,242.88 apparel buy. UndergroundShirts looks like a bulk custom-apparel vendor, though. The University of Oklahoma accounts for 35 of its 37 purchases, and this amount sits inside the vendor's typical range (median $647.75, 90th percentile $1,835). An order/invoice showing what was printed and for whom, plus the department's approval, would settle it.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.c — Personal Use: goods or services for personal use and not for official State use
result.innocent_explanation: A bulk custom-printed shirt or uniform order for the facilities/HVAC team or a department event. This is a typical use of this vendor by university buyers.

result.explanation: $20 at "CS QUIKTRIP GC" is coded as a funding transaction, which looks like a QuikTrip gift card load or cash-equivalent. Gift cards and cash are prohibited (§V.B.1.b, §V.B.1.d). This card's history shows only Amazon, Walmart, craft and similar buys. Nothing shows an employee-recognition program, which is the only gift card exception. Small amount.
result.policy_clause: §V.B.1.b — Cash, including cash advances and ATM transactions; §V.B.1.d — Gift Certificates (except purchases for employee recognition)
result.innocent_explanation: It could be a gift card bought for an employee or student recognition program, or a small fuel purchase for a non-state vehicle. Neither appears in this card's history.

result.innocent_explanation: A convenience-store snack or drink bought at a gas station chain. The card regularly buys groceries and supplies, and the MCC reflects the merchant type, not the items bought.

result.explanation: Two identical $55.22 USPS charges on consecutive days share the same PO reference (3934650238) and the same description. The card history shows no refund or credit afterward. The card has only 3 USPS transactions in 99, so there is no steady cadence that would explain a repeat. This is a likely double charge to recover.
result.policy_clause: Possible double charge: a billing error to recover, not a policy breach
result.innocent_explanation: Two separate mailings of the same First-Class letter run (e.g., a holiday mailing) could have been bought a day apart, but the shared PO reference argues against that.

result.explanation: The $521 Arkansas tax payment fits this card's pattern. The card makes mostly state tax and government payments (28 of 36 transactions). Many state revenue payments fall on the same days in June 2026, each with a different state. The merchant is used almost entirely by Oklahoma State University (25 of 26 purchases, median $465.38). I found no duplicate charge, no split, and no prohibited category.

result.innocent_explanation: Routine multi-state tax remittance by the university, paid through a payment processor on this card.

result.explanation: T202509024434 and T202509024435 are both $42.79 at WALMART.COM 8009256278 on 2025-09-19, with the same generic description. No refund or credit follows in the history, and the amount doesn't recur at a steady interval. The card does buy from Walmart.com often, which weakens the case. But nothing in the data shows two separate orders. Recover one $42.79 charge unless a receipt shows two orders.
